profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting between a faculty PI and a postdoc in an NLP lab who want to turn insights from a recent survey on neural unsupervised domain adaptation into a short workshop paper or position-plus-pilot submission. The context is that the lab has been discussing how the survey's broad claims about 'domain' and task bias could be made concrete with a small empirical study. The agenda is to generate candidate paper angles, identify a lightweight pilot experiment, and decide what existing resources can be reused. The expected outcome is a shortlist of one or two paper directions and a rough experimental sketch that feels feasible within a few weeks.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: NLP evaluation, distribution shift, benchmark design
members.background: Leads a small academic ML research group and has published on robustness audits for pretrained language models, often focusing on whether benchmark claims hold under carefully controlled evaluation.
members.private_state: She wants a conceptually sharp workshop paper that critiques loose uses of the word 'domain' in NLP adaptation, and she is wary of any empirical shortcut that could make the submission look methodologically sloppy.
hidden_assumptions: In NLP domain adaptation, a 'domain' is primarily a naturally occurring corpus or genre shift under the same task formulation, not just any change in input distribution.
A setup only counts as genuinely unsupervised if no target-domain labels are used anywhere, including for model selection, early stopping, or choosing among runs.
When people mention the 'standard Amazon sentiment benchmark,' they usually mean the classic four-domain review setup from older UDA literature.
Reusing public code means borrowing model scaffolding while harmonizing preprocessing and evaluation internally so the comparisons stay methodologically consistent.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: Large language model adaptation, benchmark reproduction, experimental pipelines
members.background: Recently joined from an industry research lab where he worked on rapid reproduction of transfer-learning papers and is comfortable stitching together released codebases to quickly get pilot results.
members.private_state: He wants a fast, credible pilot that can be assembled from existing repositories, ideally showing the lab can connect older UDA questions to modern pretrained-model settings without building a new benchmark from scratch.
hidden_assumptions: For modern NLP, any unlabeled distribution shift that changes model behavior—genre, time period, prompt format, or instruction style—can reasonably be treated as a domain.
A setup is still 'unsupervised' as long as target labels are not used to update model parameters, even if public target dev labels are used for checkpoint selection.
When researchers say the 'standard Amazon sentiment setup,' they usually mean a more recent actively maintained Amazon review transfer suite rather than the older legacy benchmark.
Reusing public code means keeping authors' default preprocessing, splits, and training scripts intact so a pilot can be produced quickly and comparably.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about testing 'different domains' and 'broadening the notion of domain.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means naturally occurring corpus or genre shifts within the same task and language, such as product reviews versus biomedical abstracts or newswire.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any unlabeled distribution shift relevant to transfer, including temporal slices, prompt formats, and instruction-style variants.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The survey itself discusses revisiting the notion of domain, so both expect some flexibility and hear the phrase as agreement rather than as a place where their boundaries differ.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'standard Amazon sentiment setup' they mean
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to using 'the standard Amazon sentiment setup' for a quick pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the classic four-domain Amazon reviews benchmark that appears throughout older domain adaptation literature.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a newer Amazon review transfer suite with different category structure, maintained code, and more recent pretrained-model baselines.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both datasets are commonly shortened to 'Amazon sentiment' in lab conversation, and because this is only a brainstorming meeting neither person feels a need to spell out the exact release.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the pilot should stay 'fully unsupervised' or 'annotation-free.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means no target labels may influence training, model selection, early stopping, or run selection in any way.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means no target labels are used in gradient-based training, but public target dev labels can still be used to pick checkpoints or settings afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse the same high-level principle, and checkpoint-selection details usually feel too low-level for early brainstorming even though they affect whether the setup truly matches the claimed regime.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'reuse the public code' to keep the pilot lightweight.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes they will borrow architectures or loaders but restandardize preprocessing, evaluation wrappers, and reporting so all comparisons share one lab-controlled protocol.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes they will run the released training and evaluation scripts largely as-is, including authors' default preprocessing and script-level choices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see code reuse as a harmless efficiency move, and the phrase sounds operationally settled even though it hides very different assumptions about standardization versus faithful replication.

turns.inner_thought: What I want is a sharp workshop paper, not a bloated empirical project. The survey was too loose about 'domain,' and that's exactly the opening: in NLP, people keep conflating real corpus or genre transfer with any arbitrary distribution change. If we can make that concrete with a small pilot across naturally occurring text sources under the same task framing, we can say something methodological without overclaiming.
turns.utterance: I've been thinking the cleanest workshop submission would be to take the survey's discussion of unsupervised domain adaptation and turn it into a concrete pilot about what we really mean by domain in NLP. Not a giant benchmark effort—more a position-plus-evidence piece.

turns.inner_thought: That works for me if we keep it lightweight. The fastest route is probably the standard Amazon sentiment setup plus one more transfer setting that feels current. We can assemble that from existing repos quickly. And if we avoid using target labels to train, I can still use the public dev labels for checkpoint selection and call it fully unsupervised the way many papers do.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that seems very doable. We could ground it with the standard Amazon sentiment setup and then add one more task so it doesn't feel too single-benchmark. If we keep the whole thing fully unsupervised, the story stays pretty clean.

turns.inner_thought: I need to steer this away from contrived shifts. The core comparison should be between genuinely different domains in the ordinary NLP sense—reviews, news, biomedical text, maybe legal if needed—not synthetic formatting tweaks. Otherwise the paper will look like it's playing word games instead of clarifying terminology.
turns.utterance: I agree, though I think the angle is strongest if we're comparing genuinely different domains rather than toy shifts. Reviews, news, biomedical text—that kind of contrast gives us something substantive to say.

turns.inner_thought: Sure, but I don't think we should artificially narrow domain. Temporal slices and instruction-style changes are exactly the kinds of distribution shifts modern models care about, and that broadening is part of what could make the paper relevant now. Also, the Amazon setup I'm thinking of already has convenient unlabeled target splits and maintained scripts, so it's a good anchor.
turns.utterance: Totally, and I think we can still be broad about it. Temporal drift and instruction-style changes could also count as domains, which might actually help connect the survey discussion to modern settings. And the Amazon setup I know already has convenient unlabeled target splits, so that piece should be easy.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the transfers are cleanly matched and we don't get lost in engineering, this can stay small. We should absolutely reuse public code, but only in the sensible way: take model scaffolding and loaders, then standardize preprocessing, evaluation, and reporting ourselves so the comparisons are actually defensible.
turns.utterance: Right. For a quick pilot, we probably don't need much more than a few clean transfers if they're matched carefully. And we should definitely reuse the public code rather than building a whole new pipeline from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then I can move fast. I'll just run the released scripts more or less as intended, keep their default preprocessing, and use the usual checkpoint-selection procedure so we get numbers by the end of the week. That's the practical meaning of reusing public code, and it's still fully unsupervised in the standard experimental sense I'm used to.
turns.utterance: Great, that makes this pretty straightforward. Then I can just run the released scripts with their default preprocessing and choose checkpoints the usual way, so we get baseline numbers fast while staying fully unsupervised.

turns.inner_thought: I should put a guardrail on this now. The paper falls apart if 'fully unsupervised' has target labels sneaking in through selection, and I don't want a patchwork of paper-specific preprocessing choices muddying the comparison. Reusing code is fine, but the lab needs a unified protocol around it.
turns.utterance: I do think the story only works if the pilot is really annotation-free on the target side. And for code reuse, what I have in mind is mostly reusing the public code for encoders and loaders, not inheriting every paper-specific evaluation choice.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine; I can still package this as a broad-domain argument. A nice three-part frame would be standard domains are too narrow: start with Amazon, then add a time-sliced news corpus, then an instruction-formatted NLI variant. That gives us a bridge from older UDA to LLM-era transfer without building anything new.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Maybe the framing is that standard domains are too narrow, and we illustrate that with three examples: Amazon, a time-sliced news corpus, and instruction-formatted NLI. Then the empirical part is small, but the conceptual point is bigger.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with that if the writeup emphasizes a classic benchmark plus a couple of clear out-of-genre transfers. The paper should argue that the survey's notion of domain needs tightening, not just expansion. If we keep the rhetoric disciplined, the pilot can support a methodological critique instead of turning into a grab bag.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's promising. The pitch could be that we pair a classic benchmark with a couple of out-of-genre transfers, then use that to show the survey's notion of domain might need tightening even if people want to broaden it.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll pull the standard benchmark suites I'm thinking of, along with their public scripts, and get candidate runs started tonight.
